title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a spectacular, cynical and sometimes shallow joyride through the American psyche
summary: Beyond an impossibly lavish presentation, the latest Grand Theft Auto game is mostly a familiar formula with some smart additions — and for the vast majority of players, it's exactly what they've…

image.caption: Lucia and Jason are the two playable characters in Grand Theft Auto VI, out Thursday on the Sony PlayStation 5 and Microsoft Xbox Series X&S consoles. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

blocks.text: For years, Grand Theft Auto VI has been many things: a meme for how long fans have been waiting for a new GTA title; a billion-dollar release; a potential spike in vacation and "sick" days; a talking point for unionization and workers' rights; a ticking cultural time bomb.
This week, finally, it's also ... a video game.

I've spent nearly 70 hours so far in GTAVI speeding across Leonida, the satirical version of Florida built by U.S.-based Rockstar Games (published by Take-Two Interactive). I've been following the story of Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, a young couple caught in a web of crime and conspiracies.

After dozens of robberies and car chases, it feels like I've only scratched the surface. But it doesn't take too long to learn that beyond an impossibly lavish presentation, this is mostly a familiar formula with some smart additions — and for the vast majority of players, it's exactly what they've been waiting for.
What's the story?

We first meet our dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, in a flashback: after a chance meeting at a carjacking, they flee the police and quickly fall in love. Flash forward and Lucia, in a moment of desperation, gets arrested after trying to rob a payday loans store.
Then we get the biggest surprise that previews have not hinted at: Jason and Lucia have a newborn boy named Tomas.

An animated gif shows the jumbo screens at Sankofa Square in Toronto displaying ads for Grand Theft Auto VI on Monday, and pedestrians walking near the EB Games store advertising the latest instalment in the video game series that launches worldwide on Thursday. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Some months after her arrest, Lucia gets out (an early release program, thanks to an overcrowded carceral state). She reconnects with Jason, and the two quickly go back to a life of crime with the ultimate goal of saving enough cash to live crime-free with their son, who is currently in Lucia's aunt's custody.

Jason and Lucia are the most convincingly realistic protagonists of the series, with sympathetic aspirations and struggles with relatable trauma, coupled with a cavalier criminal charisma and simmering chemistry that sells the fact that this is, above all, a love story.
Grand Theft Auto VI wears its crime movie influences on its sleeve. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

The same can't be said for most of the game's supporting cast. It's a parade of one-dimensional racial or regional stereotypes, nearly all of them contemptible by design: twitchy drug runners, gun-toting rap moguls and lecherous lawyers.
These types of unbelievable caricatures stick out more when placed next to the believable Jason and Lucia.
How does it look?
The word that keeps coming to mind about GTAVI's world is "astonishing."
The near-photorealistic Vice City feels like a living, breathing city, and it's surrounded by ocean beaches, swamplands and suburbs, along with a full-sized international airport terminal.
Public art adorns sections of Vice City in Grand Theft Auto VI, while the city streets are packed with drivers and citizens. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

Convenience stores feature barred windows and fading posters. Suburban lawns are frayed and worn where they meet the roads. The concrete that makes up the massive freeway networks is mottled and cracked.

You'll see non-player characters walking or sitting while having semi-realistic background conversations. Ocean Beach is packed with sunbathers of all body types, while the Jack of Hearts strip club is filled shoulder-to-shoulder with rowdy patrons and twerking models.

blocks.text: How does it play?

GTAVI's critical missions play out like a major scene in a modern summer blockbuster movie: breathtaking action and a dozen things happening (or exploding) at once. Screen wipes will zip you between Jason and Lucia's points of view as a heist goes wrong or a gang war erupts.
Unfortunately, they're also the least engaging for the player.

As Lucia struggles with a mercenary in a stairwell in a scene ripped from a John Wick movie, you'll do little more than mash the square button to get out of a chokehold. Jason might fend off a dozen armed goons, but it'll only last a few seconds before you're whisked away to another scene.

It feels more like you're strapped into an amusement park ride than an active participant, as the game desperately tries to prove that it's cool. (To be fair, it is very cool.)
Peel away the bombast and you'll find GTAVI's true strength in its conventional core: stealing cars, robbing stores and banks, and losing the cops.

Every stick-up could follow the same rough outline: flash your guns at the store clerks, intimidate security out of trying to shoot you down, before smashing and grabbing cash, jewelry and more, and getting the heck out of there as quickly as possible.

But there's always a tension with every new location: How many guards are there? Will someone on-site know the safe code, where the good stuff is? Will a jittery customer try to wrestle you down? Are the police too far away to respond, or just around the corner?
Players will make most of their money by stealing it, whether from banks, corner stores or hideouts. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
This is an open-world game, though, and familiar technical frustrations frequently show up.

Shooting and fisticuffs are competent, but clunky. Your AI-controlled companion might choose to slowly saunter to your getaway vehicle instead of jumping in, giving the cops precious few seconds to swarm you. Inventory management quickly becomes a mess, as you try to keep track of which guns Jason or Lucia are holding.

Speeding from the police or gang members can get hairy, with most cars swerving or spinning out more quickly than you might expect, until you shell out for high-end street racers or all-terrain vehicles.

blocks.text: Do I really need to buy gas for my car?
Yes, but it's only an occasional pit stop. Much has been said of the other life simulation aspects that have been added to the game.

Nearly every possible interaction will have an effect on Jason and Lucia's stats. Working out at the gym keeps their health and stamina up. Eat junk food and you'll gain weight; don't eat at all and hunger will slow your health regeneration. Even small actions like petting a cat will buff your focus meter (used to slow down time during gunfights).
Players will need to work out at the gym and eat (mostly) healthy foods to keep Jason and Lucia in peak health. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
It's a thoughtful system, but the actions aren't terribly engaging. Most gym activities simply ask you to mash or hold buttons at a certain pace, for example.

Taking the time to make Jason and Lucia hold hands, watch TV together or just give a kiss on the cheek will build their relationship meter. It's a neat bit of world-building, though ignoring it will do little to impede your journey.
How political does it get?

The GTA series has always been known for its biting satire on American culture, but even its creators have admitted the last decade's absurdities have made that more difficult, especially when things veer into the explicitly political.
To their credit, the writers walk close to that line.

A right-wing talk radio channel features a blowhard sports host who complains about trans women in sports and promises to "make sports great again." Left-wing-coded environmentalists attempt to free captive animals while spewing nonsense about energy crystals.
Tyrone, seated right, is one of your main contacts in Grand Theft Auto VI. He'll pay top dollar for stolen drugs you'll find in rival gangs' hideouts. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

Every end of the spectrum appears to be fair game, but the end result feels like blanket nihilism. Everyone is either selfish, a liar, an idiot or all three. It's hard to find truly incisive humour when the only punchline is "man, that guy sucks."

The world is full of painfully obvious knock-off brands, nearly all of them sexual innuendos or fart jokes. (The finance app on your phone is called BuckMe; a popular lemon-lime soda is called Sprunk.)
Taken individually, most of these jokes are passable. Some dialogue is laugh-out-loud hilarious. Before long, though, it becomes exhausting.

Occasionally, missions veer into gritty and even chilling drama, often revolving around the gang wars in Vice City. In momentary flashes, they're as gripping as something from The Wire; but they're jarring when placed next to gags you'd find on Family Guy.

Raul Batista leads a crew of thieves and safecracking experts in Vice City. Jason and Lucia will work with his team in a series of high-stakes heist missions in Grand Theft Auto VI. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
Can kids play it?

GTAVI is rated M for Mature (ages 17 and older) by the Entertainment Software Rating Board. Its description is a full bingo card of offensive content: blood and gore, nudity, strong language, use of drugs and more.

Gunplay is graphic, with blood and bits flying with a good headshot, though it's nothing you won't see in a modern shooter or horror game. Sexual content oscillates from romantic love scenes to churlish BDSM gags. Every swear word you can think of gets generous representation.
It's not a game for kids, obviously. Parents of teenagers will know what they can handle, but might want to play together and talk about it along the way.
Grand Theft Auto VI features several locations and regions outside of the Miami-like Vice City, including smaller suburbs and towns, swamplands and forests. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
Should you play it?
Chances are you're among the millions of people who've already pre-ordered Grand Theft Auto VI.
So while the latest GTA won't change how designers think about open-world video games, it comes in such a lavish presentation and package most players won't care.
For them, it will be more than enough to sit back on the couch while driving down Leonida's freeways at night, with neon-soaked skyscrapers in the distance as classic '80s rock plays on the radio.
